title: Quiz 2
topic: Convolution, Filtering, Noise & Feature Detection – Weeks 2 & 3

questions.text: Spatial filtering differs from intensity transformation because it:
options: Requires no mathematical operation
Works only on image borders
Uses neighboring pixels around the current pixel
Never changes pixel values
questions.answer: Uses neighboring pixels around the current pixel

questions.text: Match each padding type with its border-filling method.

pairs.definition: Mirrors image values at the image boundary
Adds zeros around the image border

questions.text: Why is padding used during convolution/filtering?
options: To remove the need for a kernel
To allow the kernel to work near image borders and help preserve output size
To classify images directly without features
To convert RGB to HSV
questions.answer: To allow the kernel to work near image borders and help preserve output size
questions.feedback: The lecture explains padding solves border-neighborhood issues and can maintain size.

questions.text: Edge detection identifies image points where:
options: The image has no useful shape information
Brightness changes sharply or discontinuities occur
The object shape changes
All pixel values are exactly equal
questions.answer: Brightness changes sharply or discontinuities occur
questions.feedback: This matches the lecture definition of edge detection.

questions.text: How does a Gaussian filter weight pixels?
options: All pixels always have exactly equal weight
Pixels closer to the center have more weight than pixels farther away
Only border pixels have weights
Pixels closer to the center have less weight than pixels farther away
questions.answer: Pixels closer to the center have more weight than pixels farther away
questions.feedback: This is the key distinction of Gaussian filtering in the lecture.

questions.text: An image gradient is:
options: A directional change in image intensity
A padding method
The same as a feature vector
Number of edges in image
questions.answer: A directional change in image intensity
questions.feedback: This is the lecture definition of an image gradient.

questions.text: Salt-and-pepper noise is visually distinctive because it appears as:
options: Very bright and very dark impulse points
Points with value larger than 255
Points from 0 to 255 value
Points from 0 to 128 value
questions.answer: Very bright and very dark impulse points
questions.feedback: The lecture describes salt-and-pepper noise as bright salt and dark pepper points.

questions.text: What happens when the smoothing mask size becomes larger?
options: The image becomes more colored
The image becomes perfectly sharper in all cases
The image becomes more smoothed/blurred and sharp details decrease
The operation becomes unrelated to filtering
questions.answer: The image becomes more smoothed/blurred and sharp details decrease
questions.feedback: The lecture shows that larger masks produce stronger blur and fewer sharp details.

questions.text: Match each concept with its correct description.

pairs.definition: Thin line darker or brighter than its neighborhood
Bright object in dark background or dark object in bright background

questions.text: Which filter sizes are mentioned as commonly used spatial filters?
options: Only 1×1 filters
Only 100×100 filters
questions.feedback: The lecture notes mention these typical small filter sizes.

questions.text: Match each filter/operator with its main role.

pairs.definition: Uses second derivative for edge/detail enhancement
Sorts values and selects the middle value
Weighted averaging with stronger center weights

questions.text: Match each noise type with its description.

pairs.definition: Very bright or very dark impulse points
Small random changes added across pixels
Small errors from rounding continuous values to digital levels
Multiplicative noise common in ultrasound and SAR

questions.text: In a 3×3 box filter, each coefficient is typically:
options: The median value
0 only
questions.feedback: The lecture example uses nine equal coefficients of 1/9.

questions.text: Gaussian noise generally affects an image by:
options: Only adding zeros around the border
Only replacing the center pixel with the median
Only detecting diagonal edges
Adding small random values across pixels
questions.answer: Adding small random values across pixels
questions.feedback: The lecture describes Gaussian noise as subtle statistical noise that alters pixels randomly.

questions.text: Median filtering is particularly effective for:
options: Only reducing image resolution
Only perfect noise-free images
Salt-and-pepper / impulse noise
Only frequency-domain filtering
questions.feedback: The lecture states median filtering is strong for spiky impulse noise.

questions.text: What is a key trade-off of smoothing filters?
options: They reduce noise but can blur edges and lose fine details
They reduce noise and edges in image
They always improve all details without any drawback
They improve edges and fine details
questions.answer: They reduce noise but can blur edges and lose fine details
questions.feedback: The lecture emphasizes this noise-detail trade-off.

questions.text: In Lecture 2, what is convolution in image processing?
options: Sliding a filter/kernel over an image, adding noise to pixels
Drawing a synthetic image from non-pictorial information
Sliding a filter/kernel over an image, multiplying corresponding values, and summing the result
Converting the continuous to discrete values
questions.answer: Sliding a filter/kernel over an image, multiplying corresponding values, and summing the result
questions.feedback: The lecture defines convolution as sliding a kernel over an image and applying multiply-and-sum at each position.

questions.text: A corner is formed when:
options: Two edges meet
Gaussian noise is present
An image is converted to HSV Color space
All pixels have the same intensity
questions.feedback: The lecture defines a corner as formed when two edges meet.

questions.text: Median filtering replaces the center pixel with:
options: Always zero
The middle value after sorting the gray levels in the mask
The filename of the image
The arithmetic average of all pixels
questions.answer: The middle value after sorting the gray levels in the mask
questions.feedback: Median filtering is based on ordering the neighborhood and choosing the middle value.

questions.text: What does the Laplacian operator compute?
options: The second derivative of the image and detects edges in either X or Y direction
The first derivative in X direction
The second derivative of the image and detects edges in all directions at once
The first derivative in Y direction
questions.answer: The second derivative of the image and detects edges in all directions at once
questions.feedback: The lecture states Laplacian computes second derivative and detects all directions at once.
